analogy.p: Imagine filling a bath while the plughole is partly blocked (the silted river) and the drain outside is full (the high tide in the Bristol Channel). The taps are the Atlantic storms, which keep running day after day. The towel on the floor already soaked through is the saturated soil: it cannot soak up any more, so the water just spills over the edge onto the floor, which is the floodplain. The analogy works because the flooding is caused by the combination of too much input and poor drainage. It breaks down because a bath has one tap and one plughole, while real flooding involves many rivers, tides and decisions by people about land and defences.

bullets: Know **what extreme weather is** and the main types that affect the UK: flooding, storms, heatwaves, drought, snow and cold snaps.
Know **evidence** that UK weather is becoming more extreme, using real figures such as temperature records.
Know **one event in depth**: where, when, what happened, the causes, the impacts and the responses.
Be able to sort impacts into **social, economic and environmental** and into **primary and secondary** effects.
Be able to explain **management strategies** (before, during and after) and judge how effective they were.
Exam questions are usually 4 or 6 marks, so you need **place-specific facts** (named rivers, villages, dates, figures).
Link to **climate change**, covered in the next two spec points, because many experts expect more extreme weather in future.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA Geography 8035 asks you to know that weather in the UK is becoming more extreme, to be able to give **evidence** for this, and to use **a case study of one recent extreme weather event in the UK** to show its **causes**, its **social, economic and environmental impacts**, and **how management strategies can reduce risk**. This is a case-study point, so the marks are won by precise, named detail rather than general statements. These notes use the **Somerset Levels floods of winter 2013 to 2014** as the main worked case study, with short alternatives (Beast from the East 2018, Storm Desmond 2015, the July 2022 heatwave) so that you can swap in whichever event your teacher used.

bullets: **Flooding** from prolonged or intense rain (river flooding, surface water flooding, coastal flooding from storm surges).
**Storms and high winds**, usually Atlantic depressions in autumn and winter; the Met Office names the most severe, for example Storm Desmond.
**Heatwaves and drought**: several days of well above average temperatures, or long periods with little rain, leading to water shortages and wildfires.
**Snow and cold snaps**, such as the Beast from the East in 2018, when very cold air arrived from Siberia.
Extreme weather is described by **how unusual** it is (a rare event, a record) and **how much damage** it causes.
The Met Office issues **weather warnings** (yellow, amber, red) based on likelihood and impact; red means danger to life is likely.
The UK is **not** the most extreme place on Earth; the point is that extreme events here are costly because the country is densely populated and not built for them.
core.h: What is extreme weather, and which types affect the UK?
core.p: **Extreme weather** is weather that is far outside the normal range for a place and time of year, and that is rare, intense or long-lasting enough to cause serious disruption, damage or danger. It is not just bad weather: what makes it extreme is how unusual and how damaging it is. The UK has a **temperate maritime climate**, so it normally has mild, changeable weather, which is why events such as 40 degrees Celsius or weeks of flooding stand out as extreme.

bullets: **Temperature records**: the UK record was 38.5 degrees Celsius at Faversham, Kent (August 2003); 38.7 degrees Celsius at Cambridge Botanic Garden in July 2019; and **40.3 degrees Celsius at Coningsby, Lincolnshire, on 19 July 2022**, the first time 40 degrees Celsius had been recorded in the UK.
The Met Office issued its **first ever red extreme heat warning** for the July 2022 heatwave.
**Rainfall records**: Storm Desmond (December 2015) set a UK record for rainfall in 24 hours, 341.4 mm at Honister Pass, Cumbria, at that time.
**Warmest years**: the UK's warmest years on record have nearly all occurred since the year 2000, so the average is rising as well as the extremes.
**Frequency of floods**: several major floods since the early 2000s (2007, 2009, 2013 to 2014, 2015, 2020) suggests more frequent flooding, although better recording also plays a part.
A good answer also gives a **limitation**: records only go back around 150 years, extreme events happened in the past too, and natural variation exists.
Evidence is stronger when **several types** agree: temperature, rainfall, number of warnings and insurance claims.
core.h: Evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme
core.p: The evidence comes from long-term records kept by the **Met Office**. Taken together, the figures suggest that the UK is getting warmer overall and that records for heat and heavy rainfall are being broken more often. Always remember that a single event cannot prove a trend: geographers look for a **pattern over many years**, which is why several different pieces of evidence are used together.

bullets: A **depression** is an area of low pressure where air rises, cools and condenses, forming cloud and rain; winds blow anticlockwise around it in the northern hemisphere.
**Air masses** affecting the UK include polar maritime (cool, showery), tropical maritime (warm, moist), tropical continental (hot, dry in summer) and polar continental (very cold in winter).
A strong jet stream across the Atlantic can bring a **conveyor belt of storms**; a jet stream that stalls or buckles can lock the UK into very hot, very cold or very wet weather for weeks.
**Blocking high pressure** (an anticyclone that stays put) can cause heatwaves and drought in summer and cold, dry weather in winter.
The UK is **densely populated** and many towns were built on floodplains, so a given amount of rain causes more damage than in an empty region.
The sea around the UK is warm for its latitude because of the **North Atlantic Drift**, which supplies moisture to Atlantic storms.
Link: this is why the **global atmospheric circulation** topic matters, because it explains where the polar front and jet stream sit.
core.h: Why the UK is vulnerable: the weather systems involved
core.p: The UK sits on the north-western edge of Europe next to the Atlantic Ocean, where **warm, moist tropical air meets cold polar air**. This produces the **polar front** and a stream of **depressions** (low pressure systems) that move east across the UK, bringing cloud, wind and rain. The **jet stream**, a fast river of air high in the atmosphere, steers those depressions. When it is strong and positioned to the south of the UK, one depression after another arrives, which is the setup for prolonged wet and stormy weather.

bullets: **Where**: the Somerset Levels and Moors, south-west England, including villages such as **Muchelney, Moorland and Burrowbridge**, and the town of Bridgwater downstream.
**When**: floods began in late December 2013 and early January 2014 and the worst of the flooding lasted until February 2014, with water remaining on some land for much longer.
**Scale**: a very large area of farmland under water for weeks, with around **600 homes** flooded across Somerset.
**Type of flooding**: mainly **river flooding** with very slow drainage, which is why the water stayed so long, along with some surface water flooding.
**Hazard type**: a hydro-meteorological hazard (a weather-related flood); it is described as a **recent** event, which is what the specification requires.
**Why it is a good case study**: it has clear physical causes, human factors that made it worse, and a long list of responses you can evaluate.
Check with your teacher whether your course used this event or a different one, and use the same structure (causes, impacts, responses) for whichever you learned.
core.h: Case study overview: the Somerset Levels floods, winter 2013 to 2014
core.p: The **Somerset Levels** are a very flat, low-lying area of south-west England between the Mendip Hills and the Quantock Hills, drained by rivers including the **Rivers Parrett, Tone and Brue**. Much of the land lies only a few metres above sea level, and some of it is below the level of high tides. During the winter of 2013 to 2014 the UK had a long run of Atlantic storms, and **southern England had its wettest winter in the Met Office's records going back to 1910** (the wettest January since 1910 for the south). The Levels flooded from early January 2014, and large areas stayed under water for weeks, into February.

bullets: **Physical cause 1**: a strong jet stream steered a **series of Atlantic storms**, so rain fell day after day with no time for rivers to recover.
**Physical cause 2**: **saturated soils** had no capacity to absorb more water, so surface runoff was high (high **runoff**, low **infiltration**).
**Physical cause 3**: the Levels are **flat and low-lying**, so water drains slowly and spreads out across the floodplain rather than flowing away.
**Physical cause 4**: high tides and storm surges in the Bristol Channel meant rivers such as the Parrett could not discharge into the sea (the river water was 'blocked' by the tide).
**Human cause 1**: rivers had become **silted up** and less deep, which reduced their capacity; many people argued that dredging had been stopped for years.
**Human cause 2**: land drainage and building on the floodplain, plus a heavy dependence on pumps to keep the land dry, meant that people lived and farmed in an area naturally at risk of flooding.
**Human cause 3**: some scientists link the pattern of more intense storms to **climate change**, although a single storm season cannot be blamed on it alone.
core.h: Causes of the Somerset floods: physical and human
core.p: The floods had **physical (natural) causes** and **human causes**, and top-mark answers explain both and show how they interacted. The main trigger was the **weather**: the jet stream was unusually strong and sat to the south of the UK, steering a sequence of deep Atlantic depressions across southern England. Each one added rain to ground that was already **saturated**, so almost all the water ran straight off into rivers instead of soaking in, and rivers that were already full burst their banks.

bullets: Around **600 homes** were flooded and many families had to leave, some living in temporary accommodation for months.
Villages such as **Muchelney were cut off** for weeks because roads were under water; food and supplies were brought in by boat and tractor and the **army** helped with sandbags and rescue.
**Roads and a main rail line were closed or disrupted**, making it hard to reach work, school, shops and health care.
**Schools closed** and some pupils could not get to lessons; community halls were used as emergency centres.
**Stress and mental health** problems were reported, including anxiety and the strain of dealing with insurance and repairs.
**Power cuts and loss of services** affected some homes; floodwater was contaminated with sewage, creating a health risk.
Strong **community spirit** was shown by volunteers, but there was also **anger** at the authorities for the speed of the response.
core.p: **Social impacts** are the effects on people's lives, health, homes and communities. In Somerset the impacts fell most on people in small, rural villages who were suddenly cut off from the outside world. Because the water stayed for weeks rather than hours, the effects lasted much longer than with a typical flash flood, and the stress and disruption were severe even for people whose homes did not flood.

bullets: **Farmland and livestock**: thousands of hectares of grazing and crop land were flooded; farmers had to move cattle, buy extra feed and lost production and income.
**Homes and businesses** suffered damage, and clean-up and repairs cost many millions of pounds across Somerset.
**Transport disruption**: closed roads (including the A361 at times) and rail disruption cost businesses time and money and delayed deliveries.
**Tourism and local businesses** lost customers, and some shops and pubs closed or lost trade for weeks.
**Insurance**: insurers paid out large sums, and some householders found their premiums rose or cover became harder to get.
**Cost to the government and agencies**: the Environment Agency, local councils and the government spent money on pumping, flood defences and compensation.
**Long-term effects**: damage to property value and the knock-on effect on the local economy lasted months after the water had gone.
core.p: **Economic impacts** are the effects on money, jobs, businesses, property and infrastructure. Farming is the main land use on the Levels, so the economy there was hit very hard, but the costs also spread across the wider region and country. Remember to separate **direct costs** (damage to buildings and land) from **indirect costs** (lost income, disruption and delays).

bullets: **Water pollution**: floodwater picked up sewage, oil, chemicals and farm waste and spread them across the land.
**Soil and farmland damage**: waterlogging, silt and debris damaged soil structure and killed crops and grass.
**Wildlife**: some animals and nests were drowned or displaced and some species were stressed, though wetland birds and fish can also benefit from temporary flooding.
**Habitats**: prolonged flooding can harm some habitats but also **recharges wetlands** that depend on regular flooding.
**Debris and waste**: floods left large amounts of waste, damaged cars and household items that had to be cleared.
**Long-term**: the flood raised debates about how to manage the Levels so that wildlife and people can both be protected.
For a balanced answer, say that wetlands are **adapted to flooding**, so the damage was greatest where pollution and the duration of the flooding were worst.
core.p: **Environmental impacts** are the effects on land, water, plants and animals. The Somerset Levels are a **wetland of great importance for wildlife**, with parts protected as Sites of Special Scientific Interest, so floods are partly a natural process there. But the unusual length of the flood and the pollution it carried caused real damage, and the impacts were not all negative.

bullets: **Immediate**: emergency services, the **army** and volunteers helped residents, filled **sandbags**, evacuated people and delivered food and medicines.
**Immediate**: the Environment Agency installed **extra high-capacity pumps** (some brought in from abroad) to remove water from the Levels, a very slow process because of the area's flatness.
**Immediate**: Met Office and Environment Agency **flood warnings** told residents which areas were at risk.
**Long-term**: the **Somerset Levels and Moors Flood Action Plan** (2014) set out a 20-year plan to reduce flood risk.
**Long-term**: **dredging** of parts of the Rivers Parrett and Tone began in 2014 to increase their capacity, along with repair and raising of **river banks** and roads.
**Long-term**: improved **pumping stations**, new flood defences, a proposed tidal barrier on the River Parrett at Bridgwater, and better land management (for example slowing runoff upstream).
**Planning**: restrictions on building in high-risk areas, and community flood plans and awareness campaigns.
core.h: Responses and management: immediate and long-term
core.p: Responses are often grouped as **immediate (short-term)** and **long-term**, and also as measures to **prevent, protect and prepare**. In Somerset, the immediate response focused on rescue, pumping and supplies, while the long-term response focused on changing how the rivers and land were managed so that the next event would do less damage.

bullets: **Dredging**: increases how much water a river channel can hold and so reduces local flooding, **but** it is expensive, needs repeating, can harm wildlife habitats and may move the flood problem **downstream**; critics said it would not have prevented a flood of this size.
**Pumping**: removes water from low land and was essential in the emergency, **but** it is slow, expensive and relies on power and maintenance.
**Hard engineering** (raised banks, barriers) protects homes directly, **but** it is costly and can give a false sense of security.
**Soft engineering and land management** (slowing runoff, restoring wetlands) is cheaper and more sustainable, **but** it works slowly and cannot fully protect settlements.
**Warnings and community plans** save lives and reduce damage at low cost, **but** only if people act on them.
**Overall**: the combination of strategies reduced risk but could not stop flooding in future extreme events; the Levels will always flood sometimes.
A balanced judgement should consider **who benefits** (residents, farmers, wildlife) and **who pays** (taxpayers, landowners).
core.h: Evaluating the management: was it effective?
core.p: The specification asks about **how management strategies can reduce risk**, and evaluating them is where Higher-level marks are earned. No single strategy removes flood risk completely, and each has costs and trade-offs. Use words like 'however', 'but' and 'in the long term' to show that you are weighing up positives and negatives rather than just listing facts.

bullets: **Beast from the East (late February to March 2018)**: very cold air from Siberia met Storm Emma, bringing heavy snow, drifting snow, very low temperatures, school closures, stranded motorists and red weather warnings in some areas; causes link to a disrupted jet stream and a high-pressure block.

**Storm Desmond (5 to 6 December 2015)**: a very deep depression brought record rainfall to Cumbria (341.4 mm in 24 hours at Honister Pass), flooding Carlisle, Cockermouth and Kendal and damaging thousands of homes, bridges and roads.

**July 2022 heatwave**: the first red extreme heat warning and **40.3 degrees Celsius** at Coningsby on 19 July 2022; impacts included rail and road disruption, wildfires, health risks for the vulnerable and strain on water supplies.
**Summer 2018 or 2022 drought**: dry ground, hosepipe bans and impacts on farming and rivers.
For any event, always give: **name and date, where, cause (the weather system), social, economic and environmental impacts, and the responses**.
Use the **same command words**: describe (what happened), explain (why), assess (weigh up) and evaluate (judge).
core.h: Other possible case studies: swap-in facts
core.p: If your school used a different event, the structure of your answer is identical. What changes are the facts, so it is worth knowing the headline points of other well-known UK events. Pick one and learn it in as much detail as the Somerset case above.

bullets: **Link to climate change**: warmer air holds more moisture, so heavy rain events may become more intense; heatwaves are expected to become more frequent and more severe.
**Link to atmospheric circulation**: the position and strength of the jet stream controls which storms reach the UK.
**Link to planning**: building on floodplains and drainage choices make a natural hazard into a disaster; the same rainfall causes more damage where more people and property are exposed.
**Link to development**: the UK is a high-income country (HIC), so it can afford warnings, defences and compensation, but costs and inequality still matter (rural communities felt neglected).
**Judgement**: you should be able to say which impacts were most significant (for example the long duration and the farming losses) and justify why.
**Prediction**: the Met Office suggests that the UK will probably have wetter winters and hotter, drier summers, so adaptation will become more important.
Use evidence in your judgement: name a place, a date or a figure to prove each point.
core.p: Top-band answers do more than state facts: they connect the event to the bigger picture and make a judgement. The most useful connection is to **climate change**, because a warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour (roughly 7 per cent more per degree Celsius), which can make heavy rainfall more intense, and warmer seas feed stronger storms. At the same time, geographers are careful: one event is **weather**, while **climate** is a long-term average, so you cannot prove that climate change caused any single event.

exam: **State/identify (1 mark)**: give one fact, such as 'the record UK temperature is 40.3 degrees Celsius' or the name of a river.
**Describe (2 to 3 marks)**: give 'what happened' with a figure or place name; one developed point earns a second mark.
**Explain (4 marks)**: make a point, then link with 'because', 'which led to' and 'this meant that'; for causes use physical **and** human reasons.
**Using a case study, assess/evaluate (6 marks)**: include a named event, at least 3 facts (a date, a place, a figure), social/economic/environmental impacts, and a **judgement** at the end.
**Graph and data questions**: quote figures with units, calculate the change, and use 'the trend' language; for a percentage change use (change divided by original) multiplied by 100.
**Evidence of more extreme weather**: always use a trend plus a limitation, such as 'but this is a short time period'.
**Model phrases**: 'prolonged heavy rainfall', 'saturated ground meant that', 'rivers exceeded their capacity', 'reduces the risk by', 'however, this is expensive'.
**Management questions**: split into **before** (preparation, planning, warnings), **during** (rescue, pumping), **after** (rebuilding, dredging) and evaluate each.
**Time management**: 6-mark questions take about 7 to 8 minutes, so plan three or four paragraphs rather than a list.
**Use the stimulus**: if a figure, photo or map is given, refer to it directly before bringing in case-study detail.

mistakes.r: Explain the **combination** of causes: a series of storms steered by the jet stream, saturated soil, flat low-lying land, silted rivers and high tides stopping the rivers draining.
mistakes.w: The Somerset floods were caused only by heavy rain.

mistakes.r: A single event is **weather**; climate is a long-term average. Say it is **consistent with** climate change, not proof of it.
mistakes.w: Extreme weather proves climate change is happening.

mistakes.r: Organise into **social, economic and environmental** and name a specific example for each, and label primary and secondary where asked.
mistakes.w: Impacts listed as one long paragraph.

mistakes.r: Use **place-specific facts**: named villages, rivers, dates and figures (for example 600 homes, Muchelney cut off).
mistakes.w: Using vague words like 'lots of damage' or 'many people'.

mistakes.r: Evaluate: dredging increases capacity but is expensive, needs repeating, can harm habitats and may only move the problem downstream.
The record is **40.3 degrees Celsius at Coningsby on 19 July 2022**, the first time 40 degrees Celsius was reached in the UK.
The spec asks for a **recent UK** event, so using Haiti or Japan will not get the marks.
mistakes.w: Giving a case study from another country.

mistakes.r: Add a judgement: say how effective each was, with a strength and a weakness, and an overall conclusion.

summary: The spec asks you to know that UK weather is becoming more extreme, to give evidence for this, and to use a case study of one recent UK extreme weather event (here the Somerset Levels floods, 2013 to 2014) to explain its causes, its social, economic and environmental impacts and how management reduces risk. It matters because it is a regular 4 and 6 mark case-study question where precise facts and evaluation earn the top marks.

terms.d: Weather that is far outside the normal range for a place and time of year, and which is rare, intense or long-lasting enough to cause serious disruption or damage.
An area of low atmospheric pressure where air rises, causing cloud, rain and strong winds; the usual cause of wet and stormy weather in the UK.
A narrow band of very fast winds high in the atmosphere that steers depressions; its strength and position affect UK weather.
An area of high pressure with sinking air, usually bringing settled, dry weather; a blocking high can cause heatwaves or cold snaps.
When water covers land that is normally dry, for example when a river exceeds its channel capacity.
The flat area of land either side of a river that is naturally covered by water when the river floods.
Soil that cannot hold any more water, so any extra rainfall runs off over the surface.
Water that flows over the land surface into rivers instead of soaking into the ground.
Removing silt and sediment from the bed of a river to make the channel deeper and increase its capacity.
A rise in sea level caused by low pressure and strong winds pushing water towards the coast.
The immediate impact of a hazard, for example flooded homes.
A later impact that results from the primary effect, such as stress, job losses or disease.
An effect on people's lives, health, safety and communities.
An effect on money, jobs, businesses, property and infrastructure.
An effect on the natural environment such as land, water, plants and animals.
Action taken during and straight after a hazard to save lives and reduce harm.
Action taken after the event to rebuild and reduce future risk.
Actions that reduce the severity or the effects of a hazard.

worked.ans: 4.7 per cent increase (the change is 1.8 degrees Celsius).
worked.q: Calculate the percentage increase from the 2003 UK record temperature (38.5 degrees Celsius) to the 2022 record (40.3 degrees Celsius). Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (3 marks)
steps: Find the change: 40.3 minus 38.5 = 1.8 degrees Celsius.
Divide by the original value: 1.8 divided by 38.5 = 0.04675...
Multiply by 100: 4.675... per cent, which is 4.7 per cent to 1 decimal place.

worked.ans: In winter 2013 to 2014 the Somerset Levels flooded because a strong jet stream steered a series of Atlantic depressions across southern England, bringing the wettest winter in the records since 1910 for the south. The ground was already saturated, so almost all the rain ran off into rivers such as the Parrett and Tone. The Levels are flat and low-lying, so the water drained slowly, and high tides in the Bristol Channel prevented rivers discharging into the sea. The rivers were also silted up, which reduced their capacity, so the water spread across the floodplain for weeks.
worked.q: Using a case study of an extreme weather event in the UK, explain the causes of the event. (4 marks)
steps: Name the event and date to anchor the answer.
Give the physical cause: the weather system and why it happened.
Add the ground conditions (saturated soil, flat land).
Add a human factor and link it to the flooding.

worked.ans: In the Somerset Levels floods of 2014, socially around 600 homes were flooded and villages such as Muchelney were cut off for weeks, which caused stress and left families in temporary accommodation. Economically, farmland and livestock were badly affected, roads and the rail line were disrupted and businesses lost trade, with costs of many millions of pounds. Environmentally, floodwater polluted land with sewage and chemicals and damaged habitats, although wetland wildlife is adapted to some flooding. Immediate responses were the army, sandbags and extra pumps, which saved homes but were slow because the land is so flat. The long-term Flood Action Plan included dredging of the Parrett and Tone and raising river banks, which increases channel capacity and reduces local flood risk. However, dredging is expensive, needs repeating and may only move flooding downstream. Overall, management reduced the risk but cannot remove it, so the most effective approach combines hard engineering with land management and warnings.
worked.q: Using a case study, assess the impacts of an extreme weather event and the effectiveness of the management. (6 marks)
steps: Name the event and where it happened.
Social: one specific impact; Economic: one; Environmental: one.
Immediate response and one long-term response.
Judgement: say how effective management was and justify it.
